title: Save the king from a known void

feedback.title: Save the king; the ace is already gone
feedback.summary: West has already shown void in Diamonds and is free to trump this trick no matter which Diamond you play; with the ace of Diamonds already out, your king is the highest Diamond left and worth keeping for a trick it can actually win.
points: The earlier trick shows West playing a club when Diamonds were led, so West holds no more Diamonds this hand and is free to trump this one.
The ace of Diamonds is already out, so the king is the highest Diamond left — a real winner if it survives to a trick West cannot trump away.
The target still needs one more trick from the two remaining; keeping the king gives the final trick a genuine winner instead of spending it here for nothing.

feedback.title: Risking your best card on a trick you don't control
feedback.summary: West's confirmed void means West decides whether this trick is trumped, regardless of which Diamond you play, so leading with the king risks your best remaining card for no extra chance of winning it.
points: The earlier trick already showed West void in Diamonds — West can trump this trick with any spade no matter which Diamond you offer.
If West trumps, the king is spent for nothing, and only the weak three is left for the final trick the target still needs.
The three loses this trick just as surely as a trumped king would, but keeps the king in hand as a genuine option for later.

author_notes: First void-tracking scenario (EC-042). The void is derived from the observed trick (West failed to follow Diamonds), never authored as a flat fact. This is the flagship case: the correct choice flips from the naive 'always lead your best card' instinct once the void is accounted for.
